query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of surface-modified graphene (Cu@Gr) to W-Mo-Cu composites can increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Addition of Cu@Gr to W-Mo-Cu composite
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform distribution of Cu phase and formation of Cu network structure
generation.mechanism: Graphene facilitates sintering densification and acts as a 'wetting bridge' for liquid Cu to infiltrate the W-Mo skeleton
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased thermal conductivity and improved microstructure with reduced porosity
generation.boundary: Optimal Cu@Gr content (0.4 wt.%) for achieving balanced properties
generation.uncertainty: Potential negative impact of carbides on electrical conductivity

falsification_experiment.design: Comparison of thermal conductivity and microstructure of W-Mo-Cu composites with and without Cu@Gr
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Cu@Gr does not result in increased thermal conductivity and improved microstructure, the hypothesis is falsified.

Figure 6 shows the SEM images of the infiltration-sintered Cu@Gr/W-Mo-Cu composites. EDS analysis of the 1 wt.% Cu@Gr-added W-Mo-Cu composite was conducted, with results shown in Figure 7. EDS analysis reveals that the white areas in the SEM image correspond to the W phase, the light gray regions primarily represent the Mo phase, and the dark gray areas were attributed to the Cu phase. The W-Mo-Cu composite without Cu@Gr contains some circular pores of varying sizes, indicating insufficient infiltration of Cu into the W-Mo skeleton during processing, which resulted in incomplete filling of interparticle voids between W and Mo. Furthermore, the distribution of Cu is also not uniform, resulting in the formation of Cu melt pools.
